## What is a Nurse Practitioner?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/4b12f07/2147483647/crop/372x244+32+0/resize/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2F10%2F859ec40b8b2f5ab184c47f651941d9%2Fjobs-job-photo-126.jpg)Median Salary$129,210Unemployment Rate 0.6%Number of Jobs 128,400

Nurse practitioners are registered nurses with additional education. Extra schooling allows these health care professionals to take patient histories, perform physical exams, order labs, analyze lab results, prescribe medicines, authorize treatment plans and educate patients and their families on continued care.   
  
Nurse practitioners, also known as advanced practice registered nurses, specialize in treating specific patient populations, training to work in areas like women's health or pediatrics. They may also work in research or academia.  
  
While their job duties sounds similar to a physician's, the main difference is the amount of formal education required.[Physicians](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/physician)have more training, and their breadth of knowledge and their salaries are usually commensurate with their additional work. However, nurse practitioners are increasingly providing primary care to patients.   
  
Many nurse practitioners first worked as[registered nurses,](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/registered-nurse)where their patient care may have extended to holistic and wellness care; they can bring that background to the diagnosis, treatment and management of medical issues.  
  
Nurse practitioners are handsomely paid for their work, with the majority taking home six-figure salaries. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 40.1% employment growth for nurse practitioners between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 128,400 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Nurse Practitioner

Future nurse practitioners spend a considerable amount of time in school. All nurse practitioners must first be registered nurses, so a bachelor's degree, associate degree or other approved diploma is a requirement. Passing the National Council Licensure Examination is also required.  
  
The next step is obtaining a master's or doctoral degree from an accredited nursing program, which can take two to four years. NPs need additional certification to use the APRN title. They must also attain board certification in their specialty, such as pediatrics, adult-gerontology or women's health. Exact requirements vary by state, so NP hopefuls should check with their state's board of nursing for certification exam details and other requirements.

## What is a Nurse Practitioner?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/4b12f07/2147483647/crop/372x244+32+0/resize/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2F10%2F859ec40b8b2f5ab184c47f651941d9%2Fjobs-job-photo-126.jpg)Median Salary$129,210Unemployment Rate 0.6%Number of Jobs 128,400

Nurse practitioners are registered nurses with additional education. Extra schooling allows these health care professionals to take patient histories, perform physical exams, order labs, analyze lab results, prescribe medicines, authorize treatment plans and educate patients and their families on continued care.   
  
Nurse practitioners, also known as advanced practice registered nurses, specialize in treating specific patient populations, training to work in areas like women's health or pediatrics. They may also work in research or academia.  
  
While their job duties sounds similar to a physician's, the main difference is the amount of formal education required.[Physicians](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/physician)have more training, and their breadth of knowledge and their salaries are usually commensurate with their additional work. However, nurse practitioners are increasingly providing primary care to patients.   
  
Many nurse practitioners first worked as[registered nurses,](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/registered-nurse)where their patient care may have extended to holistic and wellness care; they can bring that background to the diagnosis, treatment and management of medical issues.  
  
Nurse practitioners are handsomely paid for their work, with the majority taking home six-figure salaries. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 40.1% employment growth for nurse practitioners between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 128,400 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Nurse Practitioner

Future nurse practitioners spend a considerable amount of time in school. All nurse practitioners must first be registered nurses, so a bachelor's degree, associate degree or other approved diploma is a requirement. Passing the National Council Licensure Examination is also required.  
  
The next step is obtaining a master's or doctoral degree from an accredited nursing program, which can take two to four years. NPs need additional certification to use the APRN title. They must also attain board certification in their specialty, such as pediatrics, adult-gerontology or women's health. Exact requirements vary by state, so NP hopefuls should check with their state's board of nursing for certification exam details and other requirements.

## What Is a Pilot?

![Image 4](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/7d6084e/2147483647/thumbnail/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2Fed%2Fb5%2F67abbb164280bbb869f1011c6199%2Fpilotcockpit.jpg)Median Salary$226,600Unemployment Rate N/A Number of Jobs 3,900

## What is a Pilot?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/7d6084e/2147483647/thumbnail/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2Fed%2Fb5%2F67abbb164280bbb869f1011c6199%2Fpilotcockpit.jpg)Median Salary$226,600Unemployment Rate N/A Number of Jobs 3,900

Pilots fly and operate aircraft like airplanes and helicopters for airlines, private corporations, law enforcement agencies and the military. They also prepare the aircraft for flight, which includes ensuring there are no mechanical defects with the aircraft, verifying that scheduled maintenance is done and any repairs are complete, and checking the route of flight as well as departure, destination and alternate airports to make sure the flight is safe for weather conditions. Pilots also make sure the aircraft is properly balanced with passengers, cargo, baggage and fuel load.  
  
“You may be within your weight limitation, but if the balance is out, it can be very difficult to raise the nose or raise the tail if the center of gravity is off, just like on a teeter-totter,” says David Dornacker, flight simulator and academic ground school instructor at CAE USA, a major defense contractor that provides flight simulation training for the military. Dornacker was previously a pilot with ExpressJet Airlines (formerly Continental Express) for 14 years, where he served as first officer then captain, and prior to that was an air traffic controller with the U.S. Navy for 20 years.  
  
Getting the aircraft ready for takeoff is “not just a matter of loading up the aircraft and topping it off and going. You’ve got to actually have a plan; you have to know how much fuel you’re going to burn to get to your destination, you have to have reserve fuel left over to be compliant with federal air regulations, and should you need an alternate, you’ve got to have enough fuel to get to that alternate airport and then have adequate fuel reserves on board as well,” Dornacker says.  
  
Once preflight duties have been performed, pilots have the arduous job of getting the aircraft safely in the sky. Dornacker says the pilot files the route of flight, requests clearance from the air traffic controllers, takes position on the runway, runs through final checks for the aircraft, runs the power-up check on the engines, and then climbs out at the appropriate speed to get to the assigned cruising altitude.  
  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics groups pilots into two categories: airline and commercial. Airline pilots generally work on a fixed schedule for an airline as they transport people and cargo to their destinations. Commercial pilots typically perform unscheduled flights for corporations, wealthy individuals, aerial tours, charter flights and pesticide application.  
  
Ambulance services is expected to be a large area of growth among commercial pilots in the next decade, according to the BLS, as pilots will be hired to transport patients to hospitals and other health care facilities.   
  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 3.9% employment growth for pilots between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 3,900 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Pilot

A college degree isn’t a blanket requirement to become a pilot. But some airlines require a degree, so it’s recommended to give yourself the best choice of jobs in this field.   
  
Pilots receive a lot of on-the-job training, but Dornacker says, “normally, you get training from a scheduled operator trainer. There are Part 141 schools, which is a school that actually has a syllabus to it. They are moderate to expensive cost.”   
  
Military, college or civilian flight schools are the typical routes to becoming a pilot, says Shane Bise, first officer at NetJets, a private jet company based in Columbus, Ohio.   
  
“With college and civilian training, one typically starts as a student pilot and works up through their commercial pilot license,” says Bise, who is based in Cleveland.  
  
At that point, they have a few options. “Most go on to become flight instructors; however, some go on to tow banners in high tourist areas,” he says. “Sometimes, one can get lucky and find a smaller operator willing to give them a chance as a low-time pilot, but those opportunities are few and far between. After building up to between 1,000 and 1,500 hours (of actual pilot flying time), many more opportunities open up due to eligibility for the ATP license, which is the highest license available to a commercial pilot.”   
  
If a high salary is important to you, Dornacker says consider attending an aviation college, which could almost guarantee you a job after you graduate. That said, tuition and other fees could cost you well into the six figures.   
  
“It’s not very lucrative starting out because typically your first year, the salary is somewhere between the $30,000 and $50,000 range as a first officer,” he says. “As you get more senior with time, the better flying jobs come, and of course the better pay. The pay can exceed $350,000 a year now as a senior airline pilot at a place like FedEx, UPS or Delta.”   
  
If you’re considering a career as a pilot, Dornacker says you must pass a medical exam. “The first thing I would do before I put any serious money down in flight training is see if you can pass an Federal Aviation Administration Class 1 medical exam, because if you can’t, there’s no sense in spending any money on training. If you can hold a Class 2 medical but not a Class 1, at least you can become a corporate pilot. In order to work for a scheduled air carrier, you must have FAA Class 1 medical.”   
  
Pilots should also have strong math skills and a good grasp of mechanics, Bise says. “One skill that I think is often overlooked is customer service. … A pilot telling passengers what is causing a delay is such a small thing but goes a long way in conveying confidence and calmness to passengers, especially those who are nervous fliers.”  
  
Dornacker adds, “It’s good to be a good three-dimensional thinker because you’re operating in a three-dimensional environment. Let’s face it: We’re taking a very heavy aircraft/vehicle, putting it up at 37,000 feet at three-quarters the speed of sound, flying in pressurized, air-conditioned comfort. You’ve got to be able to tie all this stuff together and be a quick thinker when something does go amiss and have a solution to it.”  
  
In those quick-thinking situations, Dornacker says pilots primarily use the aircraft manuals to determine the appropriate fix and are only expected to have a few things memorized.   
  
While there’s no continuing education required as a pilot, Dornacker says, “you do have to prove yourself as an airline captain every six or nine months, depending on the air carrier and the FAA.”   
  
For that, you can expect to spend a couple days in ground school, which will cover any changes to rules and regulations, company policy updates and instruction in crew resource management. “After you do that, then you go off to the flight simulators.”

## What is a Pilot?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/7d6084e/2147483647/thumbnail/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2Fed%2Fb5%2F67abbb164280bbb869f1011c6199%2Fpilotcockpit.jpg)Median Salary$226,600Unemployment Rate N/A Number of Jobs 3,900

Pilots fly and operate aircraft like airplanes and helicopters for airlines, private corporations, law enforcement agencies and the military. They also prepare the aircraft for flight, which includes ensuring there are no mechanical defects with the aircraft, verifying that scheduled maintenance is done and any repairs are complete, and checking the route of flight as well as departure, destination and alternate airports to make sure the flight is safe for weather conditions. Pilots also make sure the aircraft is properly balanced with passengers, cargo, baggage and fuel load.  
  
“You may be within your weight limitation, but if the balance is out, it can be very difficult to raise the nose or raise the tail if the center of gravity is off, just like on a teeter-totter,” says David Dornacker, flight simulator and academic ground school instructor at CAE USA, a major defense contractor that provides flight simulation training for the military. Dornacker was previously a pilot with ExpressJet Airlines (formerly Continental Express) for 14 years, where he served as first officer then captain, and prior to that was an air traffic controller with the U.S. Navy for 20 years.  
  
Getting the aircraft ready for takeoff is “not just a matter of loading up the aircraft and topping it off and going. You’ve got to actually have a plan; you have to know how much fuel you’re going to burn to get to your destination, you have to have reserve fuel left over to be compliant with federal air regulations, and should you need an alternate, you’ve got to have enough fuel to get to that alternate airport and then have adequate fuel reserves on board as well,” Dornacker says.  
  
Once preflight duties have been performed, pilots have the arduous job of getting the aircraft safely in the sky. Dornacker says the pilot files the route of flight, requests clearance from the air traffic controllers, takes position on the runway, runs through final checks for the aircraft, runs the power-up check on the engines, and then climbs out at the appropriate speed to get to the assigned cruising altitude.  
  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics groups pilots into two categories: airline and commercial. Airline pilots generally work on a fixed schedule for an airline as they transport people and cargo to their destinations. Commercial pilots typically perform unscheduled flights for corporations, wealthy individuals, aerial tours, charter flights and pesticide application.  
  
Ambulance services is expected to be a large area of growth among commercial pilots in the next decade, according to the BLS, as pilots will be hired to transport patients to hospitals and other health care facilities.   
  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 3.9% employment growth for pilots between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 3,900 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Pilot

A college degree isn’t a blanket requirement to become a pilot. But some airlines require a degree, so it’s recommended to give yourself the best choice of jobs in this field.   
  
Pilots receive a lot of on-the-job training, but Dornacker says, “normally, you get training from a scheduled operator trainer. There are Part 141 schools, which is a school that actually has a syllabus to it. They are moderate to expensive cost.”   
  
Military, college or civilian flight schools are the typical routes to becoming a pilot, says Shane Bise, first officer at NetJets, a private jet company based in Columbus, Ohio.   
  
“With college and civilian training, one typically starts as a student pilot and works up through their commercial pilot license,” says Bise, who is based in Cleveland.  
  
At that point, they have a few options. “Most go on to become flight instructors; however, some go on to tow banners in high tourist areas,” he says. “Sometimes, one can get lucky and find a smaller operator willing to give them a chance as a low-time pilot, but those opportunities are few and far between. After building up to between 1,000 and 1,500 hours (of actual pilot flying time), many more opportunities open up due to eligibility for the ATP license, which is the highest license available to a commercial pilot.”   
  
If a high salary is important to you, Dornacker says consider attending an aviation college, which could almost guarantee you a job after you graduate. That said, tuition and other fees could cost you well into the six figures.   
  
“It’s not very lucrative starting out because typically your first year, the salary is somewhere between the $30,000 and $50,000 range as a first officer,” he says. “As you get more senior with time, the better flying jobs come, and of course the better pay. The pay can exceed $350,000 a year now as a senior airline pilot at a place like FedEx, UPS or Delta.”   
  
If you’re considering a career as a pilot, Dornacker says you must pass a medical exam. “The first thing I would do before I put any serious money down in flight training is see if you can pass an Federal Aviation Administration Class 1 medical exam, because if you can’t, there’s no sense in spending any money on training. If you can hold a Class 2 medical but not a Class 1, at least you can become a corporate pilot. In order to work for a scheduled air carrier, you must have FAA Class 1 medical.”   
  
Pilots should also have strong math skills and a good grasp of mechanics, Bise says. “One skill that I think is often overlooked is customer service. … A pilot telling passengers what is causing a delay is such a small thing but goes a long way in conveying confidence and calmness to passengers, especially those who are nervous fliers.”  
  
Dornacker adds, “It’s good to be a good three-dimensional thinker because you’re operating in a three-dimensional environment. Let’s face it: We’re taking a very heavy aircraft/vehicle, putting it up at 37,000 feet at three-quarters the speed of sound, flying in pressurized, air-conditioned comfort. You’ve got to be able to tie all this stuff together and be a quick thinker when something does go amiss and have a solution to it.”  
  
In those quick-thinking situations, Dornacker says pilots primarily use the aircraft manuals to determine the appropriate fix and are only expected to have a few things memorized.   
  
While there’s no continuing education required as a pilot, Dornacker says, “you do have to prove yourself as an airline captain every six or nine months, depending on the air carrier and the FAA.”   
  
For that, you can expect to spend a couple days in ground school, which will cover any changes to rules and regulations, company policy updates and instruction in crew resource management. “After you do that, then you go off to the flight simulators.”

## What is a Financial Manager?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/d886d7a/2147483647/crop/417x274+0+0/resize/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2Fee%2F43ab15346528c1d9c064b606f89798%2Fjobs-job-photo-33.jpg)Median Salary$161,700Unemployment Rate 1.4%Number of Jobs 128,800

Financial managers oversee the finances of major companies, agencies and other organizations. Along with their teams, they coordinate accounting and produce financial reports, cash-flow statements and profit projections. To comply with various financial laws and regulations, they must pay attention to detail. Aside from working with numbers, financial managers must also help other members of their organization understand their complex reports, which requires significant communication skills.  
  
Financial managers face a competitive job market. Those who can handle international finance and the increasingly complicated world of financial instruments and securities, including derivatives, will be the most marketable to employers.  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 14.8% employment growth for financial managers between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 128,800 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Financial Manager

Financial managers usually start by earning a bachelor's degree in finance, accounting, economics or business administration. Many also earn a master's degree in an area like business administration, finance or economics and continue getting financial management training, both on the job and off. According to the BLS, financial managers typically need at least five years of experience working in a related occupation, such as a [financial analyst](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/financial-analyst), [accountant](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/accountant) or securities sales agent. Certifications and licensures are common in the field; financial professionals who work as accountants often become certified public accountants, for example. Because managers have the responsibility of overseeing others, organizations often require them to have management training as well.

## What is a Financial Manager?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/d886d7a/2147483647/crop/417x274+0+0/resize/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2Fee%2F43ab15346528c1d9c064b606f89798%2Fjobs-job-photo-33.jpg)Median Salary$161,700Unemployment Rate 1.4%Number of Jobs 128,800

Financial managers oversee the finances of major companies, agencies and other organizations. Along with their teams, they coordinate accounting and produce financial reports, cash-flow statements and profit projections. To comply with various financial laws and regulations, they must pay attention to detail. Aside from working with numbers, financial managers must also help other members of their organization understand their complex reports, which requires significant communication skills.  
  
Financial managers face a competitive job market. Those who can handle international finance and the increasingly complicated world of financial instruments and securities, including derivatives, will be the most marketable to employers.  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 14.8% employment growth for financial managers between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 128,800 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Financial Manager

Financial managers usually start by earning a bachelor's degree in finance, accounting, economics or business administration. Many also earn a master's degree in an area like business administration, finance or economics and continue getting financial management training, both on the job and off. According to the BLS, financial managers typically need at least five years of experience working in a related occupation, such as a [financial analyst](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/financial-analyst), [accountant](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/accountant) or securities sales agent. Certifications and licensures are common in the field; financial professionals who work as accountants often become certified public accountants, for example. Because managers have the responsibility of overseeing others, organizations often require them to have management training as well.

## What is an IT Manager?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/f5cba0c/2147483647/thumbnail/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2Fbd%2F80%2F5f37c7a84105b5aff55a875b67f4%2F180919-itoffice-stock.jpg)Median Salary$171,200Unemployment Rate 1.4%Number of Jobs 101,600

Information technology managers, or computer and information systems managers, help organizations navigate the labyrinth of modern technology. These important employees have the responsibility of delivering short- and long-term visions for a company's technology needs and goals. Even though most IT managers have the technical chops to execute the various jobs of the workers they supervise, they are more likely to be spotted in a meeting room than a server room.   
  
Typical duties of an IT manager include coordinating with top executives, planning upgrades of existing software or hardware and negotiating with vendors for the service of current products or the purchase of new ones.   
  
IT managers also oversee the installation and maintenance of an organization's computer information systems, protecting the office network from hackers and malware.   
  
When the job is done well, many employees don't even notice the work involved. If you haven't had an email interruption or server meltdown in the past few months, you probably have an IT manager to thank.  
  
While the highest-profile jobs are in computer systems design, almost all organizations need IT managers, especially financial and insurance companies, manufacturing firms and the government. The growing health care industry is also expected to increase its information technology use, resulting in newly created positions. The chief growth drivers will be organizations upgrading their information technology systems to newer, faster networks and striving to avoid emerging cyberthreats. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 15.2% employment growth for it managers between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 101,600 jobs should open up.

## How to Become an IT Manager

IT managers typically need a bachelor's degree in a field like computer science or information technology, and should have a strong background in computer programming, software development and math. Companies often require IT managers to have a graduate degree, such as a Master of Business Administration.   
  
It's common for professionals in this career field to spend five to 10 years in an IT occupation before being promoted to manager, but smaller companies may require less experience. Successful IT managers can further advance to IT directors, chief technology officers and chief information officers.

## What is an IT Manager?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/f5cba0c/2147483647/thumbnail/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2Fbd%2F80%2F5f37c7a84105b5aff55a875b67f4%2F180919-itoffice-stock.jpg)Median Salary$171,200Unemployment Rate 1.4%Number of Jobs 101,600

Information technology managers, or computer and information systems managers, help organizations navigate the labyrinth of modern technology. These important employees have the responsibility of delivering short- and long-term visions for a company's technology needs and goals. Even though most IT managers have the technical chops to execute the various jobs of the workers they supervise, they are more likely to be spotted in a meeting room than a server room.   
  
Typical duties of an IT manager include coordinating with top executives, planning upgrades of existing software or hardware and negotiating with vendors for the service of current products or the purchase of new ones.   
  
IT managers also oversee the installation and maintenance of an organization's computer information systems, protecting the office network from hackers and malware.   
  
When the job is done well, many employees don't even notice the work involved. If you haven't had an email interruption or server meltdown in the past few months, you probably have an IT manager to thank.  
  
While the highest-profile jobs are in computer systems design, almost all organizations need IT managers, especially financial and insurance companies, manufacturing firms and the government. The growing health care industry is also expected to increase its information technology use, resulting in newly created positions. The chief growth drivers will be organizations upgrading their information technology systems to newer, faster networks and striving to avoid emerging cyberthreats. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 15.2% employment growth for it managers between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 101,600 jobs should open up.

## How to Become an IT Manager

IT managers typically need a bachelor's degree in a field like computer science or information technology, and should have a strong background in computer programming, software development and math. Companies often require IT managers to have a graduate degree, such as a Master of Business Administration.   
  
It's common for professionals in this career field to spend five to 10 years in an IT occupation before being promoted to manager, but smaller companies may require less experience. Successful IT managers can further advance to IT directors, chief technology officers and chief information officers.

## What is an Information Security Analyst?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/3f43efc/2147483647/thumbnail/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2F2a%2F5911b29f34beed975c4df6230d9659%2Fjobs-job-photo-112.jpg)Median Salary$124,910Unemployment Rate 0.8%Number of Jobs 52,100

Information security analysts are responsible for protecting information in an organization’s computer systems from data breaches and cyberattacks. Since lots of sensitive data is stored electronically these days, including bank account numbers and passwords, these professionals are crucial.  
  
Information security analysts may install and maintain firewalls or data encryption software, develop security standards and best practices to protect sensitive information, identify risks and vulnerabilities in an organization’s network systems, and investigate if a data breach occurs.  
  
“The opportunities are vast right now in the profession,” Casey Cegielski, a professor at Auburn University who specializes in information security, and a partner at a cybersecurity consulting firm, wrote in an email. “Every organization needs security people who have a strong industry understanding and are willing to learn technical skills and continue to grow.”  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 28.5% employment growth for information security analysts between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 52,100 jobs should open up.

## How to Become an Information Security Analyst

You’ll typically need a bachelor’s degree to work in an information security role. According to the BLS, this could be a degree in computer and information technology, or even engineering or math. But Cegielski says employers may prefer candidates with a degree in information systems.  
  
“That surprises many people because they think this role is heavily focused toward computer science,” he says. “In fact, this is a business role first. You are helping secure the business based on the regulations, compliance requirements and strategy of the organization.”  
  
Various [cybersecurity certifications](https://www.usnews.com/education/learn-cybersecurity-certifications) are available, and many companies prefer to hire certified security professionals. In addition, information security analysts must always be learning and growing with the ever-changing technology landscape, staying on top of the latest trends, issues and threats.  
  
“I am a huge advocate of continuous education in this profession,” Cegielski says. “The skills and knowledge required to be successful evolve quickly.” He specifically mentions that the Certified Information Systems Security Professional, Certified Information Systems Auditor and Certified Information Security Manager “are all very challenging credentials to earn and valuable indicators of a broader understanding of the profession.”

## What is an Information Security Analyst?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/3f43efc/2147483647/thumbnail/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2F2a%2F5911b29f34beed975c4df6230d9659%2Fjobs-job-photo-112.jpg)Median Salary$124,910Unemployment Rate 0.8%Number of Jobs 52,100

Information security analysts are responsible for protecting information in an organization’s computer systems from data breaches and cyberattacks. Since lots of sensitive data is stored electronically these days, including bank account numbers and passwords, these professionals are crucial.  
  
Information security analysts may install and maintain firewalls or data encryption software, develop security standards and best practices to protect sensitive information, identify risks and vulnerabilities in an organization’s network systems, and investigate if a data breach occurs.  
  
“The opportunities are vast right now in the profession,” Casey Cegielski, a professor at Auburn University who specializes in information security, and a partner at a cybersecurity consulting firm, wrote in an email. “Every organization needs security people who have a strong industry understanding and are willing to learn technical skills and continue to grow.”  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 28.5% employment growth for information security analysts between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 52,100 jobs should open up.

## How to Become an Information Security Analyst

You’ll typically need a bachelor’s degree to work in an information security role. According to the BLS, this could be a degree in computer and information technology, or even engineering or math. But Cegielski says employers may prefer candidates with a degree in information systems.  
  
“That surprises many people because they think this role is heavily focused toward computer science,” he says. “In fact, this is a business role first. You are helping secure the business based on the regulations, compliance requirements and strategy of the organization.”  
  
Various [cybersecurity certifications](https://www.usnews.com/education/learn-cybersecurity-certifications) are available, and many companies prefer to hire certified security professionals. In addition, information security analysts must always be learning and growing with the ever-changing technology landscape, staying on top of the latest trends, issues and threats.  
  
“I am a huge advocate of continuous education in this profession,” Cegielski says. “The skills and knowledge required to be successful evolve quickly.” He specifically mentions that the Certified Information Systems Security Professional, Certified Information Systems Auditor and Certified Information Security Manager “are all very challenging credentials to earn and valuable indicators of a broader understanding of the profession.”

Among the top 10 best jobs for 2026, software developer carries the highest number of anticipated new jobs.

To choose a career, job seekers need to make a range of decisions about their personal priorities, strengths and goals.

But there are some more universal, data-driven factors that can help identify worthwhile jobs in the marketplace. That's where U.S. News' Best Jobs rankings come in.

To identify the best jobs for 2026, [U.S. News evaluated occupations](https://careers.usnews.com/advice/articles/how-us-news-ranks-the-best-jobs) in a range of industries – including [health care,](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-healthcare-jobs)[engineering](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-engineering-jobs) and [construction](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-construction-jobs) – weighing median salary, predicted growth and unemployment rate, among other factors. Data comes from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and is analyzed by U.S. News.

Careers in the STEM fields – science, technology, engineering and math – continue to dominate this list. Read on for the best jobs of 2026.

## 10. Pilot

**Industry:**Social services  
**Median salary:**$226,600  
**Unemployment rate:**N/A  
**Job growth:**3.9%, or 3,900 new jobs by 2034

Airline pilots transport passengers and cargo by operating aircraft, including airplanes and helicopters. While growth isn't sky-high in this profession, a median salary topping $225,000 is the highest on this list.

Learn more about [pilots](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/pilot).

## 9. Speech-Language Pathologist

**Industry:**Health care  
**Median salary:**$95,410  
**Unemployment rate:**0.7%  
**Job growth:**15%, or 28,100 new jobs by 2034

These health care professionals evaluate and treat patients with speech, language and other disorders. They may work in medical facilities or educational centers, providing counseling and treatment for clients.

Learn more about [speech-language pathologists](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/speech-language-pathologist).

## 8. Data Scientist

**Industry:**Technology  
**Median salary:**$112,590  
**Unemployment rate:**N/A  
**Job growth:**33.5%, or 82,400 new jobs by 2034

Data scientists analyze data to extract meaningful takeaways for businesses and organizations. Math, computer and analytical skills are essential in this field, but the ability to communicate and collaborate is also critical. A six-figure median salary and skyrocketing job growth (the second-highest on this list) contribute to making data scientist a top job for 2026.

Learn more about [data scientists](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/data-scientist).

## 7. Software Developer

**Industry:**Technology  
**Median salary:**$133,080  
**Unemployment rate:**3.1%  
**Job growth:**15.8%, or 267,600 new jobs by 2034

Software developers are the tech experts who develop, recommend and maintain software systems and upgrades. They may need to write code and work collaboratively to fix bugs and serve an organization's needs. Among the top 10 best jobs for 2026, this profession carries the highest number of anticipated new jobs, with more than 267,600 new roles expected by 2034. That said, its unemployment rate has ticked up since last year, from 2.4% to 3.4% in the 2026 rankings.

Learn more about [software developers.](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/software-developer)

## 6. Medical and Health Services Manager

**Industry:**Health care support  
**Median salary:**$117,960  
**Unemployment rate:**1.5%  
**Job growth:**23.2%, or 142,900 new jobs by 2034

Medical and health services managers focus on the administrative and management work required to run a medical facility or health care office. They may develop work schedules or manage financial tasks, working in places such as hospitals, nursing homes or group practices.

Learn more about [medical and health services managers](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/medical-and-health-services-manager).

## 5. Physician Assistant

**Industry:**Health care  
**Median salary:**$133,260  
**Unemployment rate:**1.6%  
**Job growth:**20.3%, or 33,100 new jobs by 2034

Physician assistants work as part of a health care team, diagnosing and treating patients for a range of illnesses, injuries and medical issues. They may focus on a particular specialty such as primary care or emergency medicine. Job growth for this essential health care role is expected to be particularly high in the coming years.

Learn more about [physician assistants](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/physician-assistant).

## 4. Information Security Analyst

**Industry:**Technology  
**Median salary:**$124,910  
**Unemployment rate:**0.8%  
**Job growth:**28.5%, or 52,100 new jobs by 2034

To combat cyberthreats and security breaches, information security analysts work within organizations to create and deploy security systems. They must stay abreast of the latest virtual threats and continually monitor and research vulnerabilities in computer networks and systems.

Learn more about [information security analysts](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/information-security-analyst).

## 3. IT Manager

**Industry:**Technology  
**Median salary:**$171,200  
**Unemployment rate:**1.4%  
**Job growth:**15.2%, or 101,600 new jobs by 2034

IT managers help steer an organization's use of computers and other technologies, analyzing hardware and software needs, planning upgrades, and tallying technology costs. IT refers to information technology. For this important work, they earn a median salary well into the six figures.

Learn more about [IT managers](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/it-manager).

## 2. Financial Manager

**Industry:**Business  
**Median salary:**$161,700  
**Unemployment rate:**1.4%  
**Job growth:**14.8%, or 128,800 new jobs by 2034

Financial managers claim the top business-sector job on the U.S. News Best Jobs list. These money pros manage the financial activities of a business or organization, analyzing data, pinpointing trends and advising business leaders.

Learn more about [financial managers](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/financial-manager).

## 1. Nurse Practitioner

**Industry:**Health care  
**Median salary:**$129,210  
**Unemployment rate:**0.6%  
**Job growth:**40.1%, or 128,400 new jobs by 2034

For the third consecutive year, the No. 1 job is nurse practitioner. These highly paid, highly educated, highly sought-after professionals care for patients, completing physical exams, analyzing lab results and prescribing medications. NPs often specialize in a certain patient type, such as pediatric or geriatric populations, and many work independently, consulting with physicians when needed. Explosive job growth, a low unemployment rate and robust pay help buoy this career to the top spot.

Learn more about [nurse practitioners](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/nurse-practitioner).

Among the top 10 best jobs for 2026, software developer carries the highest number of anticipated new jobs.

To choose a career, job seekers need to make a range of decisions about their personal priorities, strengths and goals.

But there are some more universal, data-driven factors that can help identify worthwhile jobs in the marketplace. That's where U.S. News' Best Jobs rankings come in.

To identify the best jobs for 2026, [U.S. News evaluated occupations](https://careers.usnews.com/advice/articles/how-us-news-ranks-the-best-jobs) in a range of industries – including [health care,](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-healthcare-jobs)[engineering](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-engineering-jobs) and [construction](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-construction-jobs) – weighing median salary, predicted growth and unemployment rate, among other factors. Data comes from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and is analyzed by U.S. News.

Careers in the STEM fields – science, technology, engineering and math – continue to dominate this list. Read on for the best jobs of 2026.

## 10. Pilot

**Industry:**Social services  
**Median salary:**$226,600  
**Unemployment rate:**N/A  
**Job growth:**3.9%, or 3,900 new jobs by 2034

Airline pilots transport passengers and cargo by operating aircraft, including airplanes and helicopters. While growth isn't sky-high in this profession, a median salary topping $225,000 is the highest on this list.

Learn more about [pilots](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/pilot).

## 9. Speech-Language Pathologist

**Industry:**Health care  
**Median salary:**$95,410  
**Unemployment rate:**0.7%  
**Job growth:**15%, or 28,100 new jobs by 2034

These health care professionals evaluate and treat patients with speech, language and other disorders. They may work in medical facilities or educational centers, providing counseling and treatment for clients.

Learn more about [speech-language pathologists](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/speech-language-pathologist).

## 8. Data Scientist

**Industry:**Technology  
**Median salary:**$112,590  
**Unemployment rate:**N/A  
**Job growth:**33.5%, or 82,400 new jobs by 2034

Data scientists analyze data to extract meaningful takeaways for businesses and organizations. Math, computer and analytical skills are essential in this field, but the ability to communicate and collaborate is also critical. A six-figure median salary and skyrocketing job growth (the second-highest on this list) contribute to making data scientist a top job for 2026.

Learn more about [data scientists](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/data-scientist).

[Best STEM Jobs](https://careers.usnews.com/best-jobs/rankings/best-stem-jobs)

## 7. Software Developer

**Industry:**Technology  
**Median salary:**$133,080  
**Unemployment rate:**3.1%  
**Job growth:**15.8%, or 267,600 new jobs by 2034

Software developers are the tech experts who develop, recommend and maintain software systems and upgrades. They may need to write code and work collaboratively to fix bugs and serve an organization's needs. Among the top 10 best jobs for 2026, this profession carries the highest number of anticipated new jobs, with more than 267,600 new roles expected by 2034. That said, its unemployment rate has ticked up since last year, from 2.4% to 3.4% in the 2026 rankings.

Learn more about [software developers.](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/software-developer)

## 6. Medical and Health Services Manager

**Industry:**Health care support  
**Median salary:**$117,960  
**Unemployment rate:**1.5%  
**Job growth:**23.2%, or 142,900 new jobs by 2034

Medical and health services managers focus on the administrative and management work required to run a medical facility or health care office. They may develop work schedules or manage financial tasks, working in places such as hospitals, nursing homes or group practices.

Learn more about [medical and health services managers](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/medical-and-health-services-manager).

## 5. Physician Assistant

**Industry:**Health care  
**Median salary:**$133,260  
**Unemployment rate:**1.6%  
**Job growth:**20.3%, or 33,100 new jobs by 2034

Physician assistants work as part of a health care team, diagnosing and treating patients for a range of illnesses, injuries and medical issues. They may focus on a particular specialty such as primary care or emergency medicine. Job growth for this essential health care role is expected to be particularly high in the coming years.

Learn more about [physician assistants](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/physician-assistant).

## 4. Information Security Analyst

**Industry:**Technology  
**Median salary:**$124,910  
**Unemployment rate:**0.8%  
**Job growth:**28.5%, or 52,100 new jobs by 2034

To combat cyberthreats and security breaches, information security analysts work within organizations to create and deploy security systems. They must stay abreast of the latest virtual threats and continually monitor and research vulnerabilities in computer networks and systems.

Learn more about [information security analysts](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/information-security-analyst).

[Best Technology Jobs](https://careers.usnews.com/best-jobs/rankings/best-technology-jobs)

## 3. IT Manager

**Industry:**Technology  
**Median salary:**$171,200  
**Unemployment rate:**1.4%  
**Job growth:**15.2%, or 101,600 new jobs by 2034

IT managers help steer an organization's use of computers and other technologies, analyzing hardware and software needs, planning upgrades, and tallying technology costs. IT refers to information technology. For this important work, they earn a median salary well into the six figures.

Learn more about [IT managers](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/it-manager).

## 2. Financial Manager

**Industry:**Business  
**Median salary:**$161,700  
**Unemployment rate:**1.4%  
**Job growth:**14.8%, or 128,800 new jobs by 2034

Financial managers claim the top business-sector job on the U.S. News Best Jobs list. These money pros manage the financial activities of a business or organization, analyzing data, pinpointing trends and advising business leaders.

Learn more about [financial managers](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/financial-manager).

## 1. Nurse Practitioner

**Industry:**Health care  
**Median salary:**$129,210  
**Unemployment rate:**0.6%  
**Job growth:**40.1%, or 128,400 new jobs by 2034

For the third consecutive year, the No. 1 job is nurse practitioner. These highly paid, highly educated, highly sought-after professionals care for patients, completing physical exams, analyzing lab results and prescribing medications. NPs often specialize in a certain patient type, such as pediatric or geriatric populations, and many work independently, consulting with physicians when needed. Explosive job growth, a low unemployment rate and robust pay help buoy this career to the top spot.

Learn more about [nurse practitioners](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/nurse-practitioner).

## What is a Software Developer?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/af66e3c/2147483647/crop/2000x1313+0+0/resize/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2Ff9%2Ff1%2Fa6174c87479b8222c09903d7651c%2F190219-softwaredevelopers-stock.jpg)Median Salary$133,080Unemployment Rate 3.1%Number of Jobs 267,700

Software developers invent the technologies we sometimes take for granted. For instance, that app that rings, sings or buzzes you out of a deep sleep every morning? A software developer helped design that. And when you roll into the office and turn on your computer, clicking and scrolling through social media, music and your personal calendar – developers had a big hand in shaping those, too.   
  
You might spend your lunch break shopping, and before you make that big purchase, you check your bank account balance using your phone. Later, you cook a new recipe from that great app your friend told you about. As you look over the course of your day, you come to see that software developers are the masterminds behind the technologies you can't imagine living without.  
  
The best developers are creative and have the technical expertise to carry out innovative ideas. You might expect software developers to sit at their desks designing programs all day – and they do, but their job involves many more responsibilities. They may spend their days working on a client project from scratch and writing new code. But they may also be tasked with maintaining or improving the code for programs that are already up and running.   
  
Software developers also check for bugs in software. And although the job does involve extreme concentration and chunks of uninterrupted time, developers have to collaborate with others, including fellow developers, managers or clients. Developers are often natural problem solvers who possess strong analytical skills and the ability to think outside the box.  
  
Software developers are employed in a range of industries, including computer systems design, manufacturing and finance. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 15.8% employment growth for software developers between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 267,700 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Software Developer

While several different paths can lead to a career in software development, here’s how many developers get started:  
  
**1. Earn a bachelor's degree.**Software developers often pursue a degree in [computer science](https://www.usnews.com/education/best-graduate-schools/articles/2019-05-02/what-can-you-do-with-a-computer-science-degree), where they study computers and programming.  
**2. Gain hands-on experience.**Employers are typically drawn to applicants with practical experience. Many students complete an internship or seek out experience beyond the classroom to prepare themselves for a career in software development. Even if you don't enroll in a formal internship program, familiarizing yourself with [coding](https://www.usnews.com/education/learn-coding-guide) and learning programming languages like [Python](https://www.usnews.com/education/learn-python-guide) and [SQL](https://www.usnews.com/education/learn-sql-guide) can show potential employers that you're equipped to do the job.  
**3. Pursue a master’s degree.**Though not required, some employers prefer developers with an advanced degree.   
  
"It's super important to understand CS fundamentals like big O notation, common algorithms, standard languages and technical approaches. You can learn this from school or from apprenticeship, but you need to learn it somehow," Sam Schillace writes in an email. Schillace is a former vice president of engineering for industry solutions at Google. Before that, he co-founded Writely, which he later sold to Google, where it was used to create Google Docs.   
  
So while a bachelor's degree in computer science is a good idea, a degree alone won't help you snag that dream job in software development. "We look at track records as much as school – someone from a great school with no outside coding projects or interesting technical accomplishments is definitely less interesting, and someone who is a rock star coder with no degree but a huge list of achievements would be an easy hire," Schillace explains.

## What is a Software Developer?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/af66e3c/2147483647/crop/2000x1313+0+0/resize/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2Ff9%2Ff1%2Fa6174c87479b8222c09903d7651c%2F190219-softwaredevelopers-stock.jpg)Median Salary$133,080Unemployment Rate 3.1%Number of Jobs 267,700

Software developers invent the technologies we sometimes take for granted. For instance, that app that rings, sings or buzzes you out of a deep sleep every morning? A software developer helped design that. And when you roll into the office and turn on your computer, clicking and scrolling through social media, music and your personal calendar – developers had a big hand in shaping those, too.   
  
You might spend your lunch break shopping, and before you make that big purchase, you check your bank account balance using your phone. Later, you cook a new recipe from that great app your friend told you about. As you look over the course of your day, you come to see that software developers are the masterminds behind the technologies you can't imagine living without.  
  
The best developers are creative and have the technical expertise to carry out innovative ideas. You might expect software developers to sit at their desks designing programs all day – and they do, but their job involves many more responsibilities. They may spend their days working on a client project from scratch and writing new code. But they may also be tasked with maintaining or improving the code for programs that are already up and running.   
  
Software developers also check for bugs in software. And although the job does involve extreme concentration and chunks of uninterrupted time, developers have to collaborate with others, including fellow developers, managers or clients. Developers are often natural problem solvers who possess strong analytical skills and the ability to think outside the box.  
  
Software developers are employed in a range of industries, including computer systems design, manufacturing and finance. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 15.8% employment growth for software developers between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 267,700 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Software Developer

While several different paths can lead to a career in software development, here’s how many developers get started:  
  
**1. Earn a bachelor's degree.**Software developers often pursue a degree in [computer science](https://www.usnews.com/education/best-graduate-schools/articles/2019-05-02/what-can-you-do-with-a-computer-science-degree), where they study computers and programming.  
**2. Gain hands-on experience.**Employers are typically drawn to applicants with practical experience. Many students complete an internship or seek out experience beyond the classroom to prepare themselves for a career in software development. Even if you don't enroll in a formal internship program, familiarizing yourself with [coding](https://www.usnews.com/education/learn-coding-guide) and learning programming languages like [Python](https://www.usnews.com/education/learn-python-guide) and [SQL](https://www.usnews.com/education/learn-sql-guide) can show potential employers that you're equipped to do the job.  
**3. Pursue a master’s degree.**Though not required, some employers prefer developers with an advanced degree.   
  
"It's super important to understand CS fundamentals like big O notation, common algorithms, standard languages and technical approaches. ## What is a Physician Assistant?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/c9fe29f/2147483647/crop/424x278+0+0/resize/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2F2f%2F717d5273c019191e4ba0cee3467a41%2Fjobs-job-photo-119.jpg)Median Salary$133,260Unemployment Rate 1.6%Number of Jobs 33,200

Physician assistants, also known as physician associates, are ubiquitous in the medical world. They use their medical expertise to examine, diagnose and treat patients, working closely with other health care professionals as a team to provide patient care.  
  
Jennifer M. Orozco, American Academy of Physician Associates chief medical officer, says physician assistants “help fill in a lot of access gaps across the country.”  
  
“They practice medicine in every health care setting, from hospitals to emergency rooms to private practice to operating suites,” Orozco says. “They take care of a patient in every specialty, from primary care to pediatrics all the way through geriatrics and palliative care.”  
  
While specific duties depend on factors including setting, specialty and state laws, physician assistants can take medical histories, assist in surgeries, conduct physical exams, prescribe medication, perform clinical research and more, according to the AAPA.  
  
“The team-based model is the hallmark of our profession,” Orozco says. “It’s who we are and really it’s about us keeping that commitment to our patients because we know that our patients’ needs are first. And patients have better outcomes when they have a team-based approach to care.”  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 20.4% employment growth for physician assistants between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 33,200 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Physician Assistant

While some physician assistants pursue a doctoral degree, the terminal degree to become a PA is a master’s. To gain admission into a physician assistant program in the U.S., students should have a bachelor’s degree from an accredited program with a strong background in science and medical courses, as well as hands-on experience caring for patients.  
  
“PA students, on average, have about 3,000 hours of direct patient care prior to coming to PA school,” Orozco says. “So they’re paramedics, they’re [nurses](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/registered-nurse), (or) they could be athletic trainers.”  
  
The amount of hours of clinical experience required for acceptance varies by program and school.  
  
Physician assistant programs typically take about three academic years (roughly 27 months) and include a blend of classroom instruction and more than 2,000 hours of clinical rotations, according to the AAPA. After graduation, PA hopefuls must take the Physician Assistant National Certifying Exam, administered by the National Commission on Certification of Physician Assistants.  
  
Physician assistants need 100 credit hours of continuing education every two years and must take a recertifying exam every 10 years to maintain their certification. They must be licensed in the state or territory in which they want to practice and see patients.

## What is a Physician Assistant?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/c9fe29f/2147483647/crop/424x278+0+0/resize/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2F2f%2F717d5273c019191e4ba0cee3467a41%2Fjobs-job-photo-119.jpg)Median Salary$133,260Unemployment Rate 1.6%Number of Jobs 33,200

Physician assistants, also known as physician associates, are ubiquitous in the medical world. They use their medical expertise to examine, diagnose and treat patients, working closely with other health care professionals as a team to provide patient care.  
  
Jennifer M. Orozco, American Academy of Physician Associates chief medical officer, says physician assistants “help fill in a lot of access gaps across the country.”  
  
“They practice medicine in every health care setting, from hospitals to emergency rooms to private practice to operating suites,” Orozco says. “They take care of a patient in every specialty, from primary care to pediatrics all the way through geriatrics and palliative care.”  
  
While specific duties depend on factors including setting, specialty and state laws, physician assistants can take medical histories, assist in surgeries, conduct physical exams, prescribe medication, perform clinical research and more, according to the AAPA.  
  
“The team-based model is the hallmark of our profession,” Orozco says. “It’s who we are and really it’s about us keeping that commitment to our patients because we know that our patients’ needs are first. And patients have better outcomes when they have a team-based approach to care.”  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 20.4% employment growth for physician assistants between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 33,200 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Physician Assistant

While some physician assistants pursue a doctoral degree, the terminal degree to become a PA is a master’s. To gain admission into a physician assistant program in the U.S., students should have a bachelor’s degree from an accredited program with a strong background in science and medical courses, as well as hands-on experience caring for patients.  
  
“PA students, on average, have about 3,000 hours of direct patient care prior to coming to PA school,” Orozco says. “So they’re paramedics, they’re [nurses](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/registered-nurse), (or) they could be athletic trainers.”  
  
The amount of hours of clinical experience required for acceptance varies by program and school.  
  
Physician assistant programs typically take about three academic years (roughly 27 months) and include a blend of classroom instruction and more than 2,000 hours of clinical rotations, according to the AAPA. After graduation, PA hopefuls must take the Physician Assistant National Certifying Exam, administered by the National Commission on Certification of Physician Assistants.  
  
Physician assistants need 100 credit hours of continuing education every two years and must take a recertifying exam every 10 years to maintain their certification. They must be licensed in the state or territory in which they want to practice and see patients.

Read pages for a research assistant. Preserve this source's evidence and follow
useful page links to fill missing fields. You do not decide the final answer.

Extraction and navigation are separate. During extraction, only the supplied page
is evidence. The original question specifies the fields to look for; it does not
establish facts. During navigation, parent notes and earlier reasoning can guide
link selection, but must not be copied into the current page's evidence.

Extract what this page can establish even if it cannot answer the whole question.
Preserve exact names, titles, dates, values, units and relevant lists. For tables,
keep each value attached to its entity and header, including year, variant and
population. Distinguish different measurements and totals from subgroups. Quote
short supporting text. Report missing fields as unknown. If the supplied page is
truncated, do not claim its unseen rows or candidates are absent. Describe list
coverage and date range so partial evidence cannot be mistaken for a complete set.

The current-page note is saved before navigation. Follow a page link when its label,
surrounding text or an observed same-site URL pattern suggests it can fill a
specific missing field. State that field and why the next page should supply it.
A relevant index may contain useful links without answer facts. A wrong-year page
can help if it links to the required year. Generic footer links on unrelated pages,
missing pages and repeated content do not justify expansion. After an unhelpful
child, choose a different supported route or stop. You may follow links outside
the menu and infer another address within a site already being read.

Child notes are preserved separately and returned automatically. Never rewrite
them as your own evidence. Keep useful Next links in your note even if the local
expansion budget is exhausted; unvisited links are not disqualified candidates.

For extraction return plain text/Markdown in this format:
**Final Information**
**Page:** Actual title and original URL.
**Evidence:** Relevant facts, lists or rows with exact fields and short source quotes.
**Coverage:** Which entities, years and conditions this page actually covers;
whether the supplied evidence is a full list, a subset, or a truncated excerpt.
**Missing:** Requested fields not established by this page.
**Next links:** Useful source URLs and the missing field each could establish.
**Expand:** yes or no, with a concrete reason.
**Status:** partial

Use answered only if this page supplies all requested facts; partial for useful
incomplete evidence; not_found for no relevant evidence, describing the page or
access error briefly. During navigation, call web_fetch or reply DONE.

## What is a Medical and Health Services Manager?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/9b88860/2147483647/crop/3867x2538+0+5/resize/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2F71%2F23%2F493d2b294d90bb038b308f1ae57d%2F151106-stock.jpg)Median Salary$117,960Unemployment Rate 1.5%Number of Jobs 142,900

Medical and health services managers are the planners, directors and coordinators who work behind the scenes to keep hospitals, nursing homes, group practices and other health care facilities running efficiently. In short, they are super-organized professionals.  
  
Medical and health services managers are extremely detail-oriented people with good analytical skills. Because much of their time is spent working with doctors, health insurance representatives and other administrators, they should also have good interpersonal and communication skills. Problem-solving is another part of the job. Technical skills are also required for these professionals to stay up-to-date on new software and electronic health record technology.  
  
The high demand for more medical and health services managers is driven by the large baby boomer population needing more health care in hospitals, group practices and nursing homes as they age. It’s also driven by the uptick in group practices and the need for managers and administrators to helm these facilities.  
  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 23.2% employment growth for medical and health services managers between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 142,900 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Medical and Health Services Manager

Most medical and health services managers have at least a bachelor’s degree in health administration. However, a master’s degree in public administration, business administration or public health might help open the door to more opportunities.  
  
Certification isn't a requirement, but it can help demonstrate proficiency to potential employers. Organizations including the Professional Association of Health Care Office Management and the American Health Information Management Association offer various certifications for medical and health services managers.   
  
“Their real-world exposure coupled with professional certification makes them a far better employment candidate than those without,” Karen Blanchette, executive director of the Professional Association of Health Care Office Management, says of professionals who obtain certification.   
  
Depending on their workplace, prospective medical and health services managers might also need to acquire licensure. For instance, nursing home administrators must be licensed, and the licensure requirements for those in charge of assisted living facilities vary by state. Some other sectors of medical and health services management don’t require licensure.

## What is a Medical and Health Services Manager?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/9b88860/2147483647/crop/3867x2538+0+5/resize/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2F71%2F23%2F493d2b294d90bb038b308f1ae57d%2F151106-stock.jpg)Median Salary$117,960Unemployment Rate 1.5%Number of Jobs 142,900

Medical and health services managers are the planners, directors and coordinators who work behind the scenes to keep hospitals, nursing homes, group practices and other health care facilities running efficiently. In short, they are super-organized professionals.  
  
Medical and health services managers are extremely detail-oriented people with good analytical skills. Because much of their time is spent working with doctors, health insurance representatives and other administrators, they should also have good interpersonal and communication skills. Problem-solving is another part of the job. Technical skills are also required for these professionals to stay up-to-date on new software and electronic health record technology.  
  
The high demand for more medical and health services managers is driven by the large baby boomer population needing more health care in hospitals, group practices and nursing homes as they age. It’s also driven by the uptick in group practices and the need for managers and administrators to helm these facilities.  
  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 23.2% employment growth for medical and health services managers between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 142,900 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Medical and Health Services Manager

Most medical and health services managers have at least a bachelor’s degree in health administration. However, a master’s degree in public administration, business administration or public health might help open the door to more opportunities.  
  
Certification isn't a requirement, but it can help demonstrate proficiency to potential employers. Organizations including the Professional Association of Health Care Office Management and the American Health Information Management Association offer various certifications for medical and health services managers.   
  
“Their real-world exposure coupled with professional certification makes them a far better employment candidate than those without,” Karen Blanchette, executive director of the Professional Association of Health Care Office Management, says of professionals who obtain certification.   
  
Depending on their workplace, prospective medical and health services managers might also need to acquire licensure. For instance, nursing home administrators must be licensed, and the licensure requirements for those in charge of assisted living facilities vary by state. Some other sectors of medical and health services management don’t require licensure.

## What is a Dentist?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/a43237c/2147483647/thumbnail/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2F02%2Fb5%2F1c3123f449aeb8db06f505ec8710%2Fdentist.jpg)Median Salary$172,790Unemployment Rate N/A Number of Jobs 5,400

Dentists identify and treat problems concerning a patient's mouth, gums and teeth. Their duties include extracting teeth, fitting dentures and filling cavities. Some choose to specialize in areas that range from treating serious oral problems and diseases to straightening teeth and performing oral surgeries. They are assisted by [dental hygienists](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/dental-hygienist "Link: https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/dental-hygienist"), who complete a patient's teeth cleaning, and by [dental assistants](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/dental-assistant "Link: https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/dental-assistant"), who usually help with record keeping and instrument sterilization.  
  
Many people dread the dentist. When they open wide, they're afraid what the dentist will find. Yet another cavity? Or even worse – will it be time for a root canal? Will the dentist embarrass them about their flossing frequency or their coffee drinking? Will they push procedures that patients don't want?  
  
According to Ada S. Cooper, a consumer adviser for the American Dental Association and dentist with a private practice in New York City, these concerns are why establishing trust is so important. "Patients have to know that dentists are doing what's best for them," Cooper says. And they can do this by being honest, ethical and compassionate – three qualities Cooper looks for when she is hiring at her practice. She also highlights the importance of good communication skills.  
  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 4.1% employment growth for dentists between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 5,400 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Dentist

Becoming a dentist involves a marathon of training and testing. Ideally, the pathway starts as early as high school, when you focus on Advanced Placement courses in chemistry, physics, biology and mathematics. Here are the next steps to take:  
  
**1. Get an undergraduate degree.** As undergrads, aspiring dentists will need to take a host of premedical courses in mathematics, chemistry and biology. Aspiring dentists will also need to acquire top marks in undergrad and glowing letters of recommendation to get into dental school.  
**2. Take the Dental Admission Test.** Most dentists take the DAT by their junior year. Getting into dental school is competitive, and scoring well on the acceptance test is only one of the hurdles.  
**3. Attend dental school.**Dental school itself is a rigorous mix of practical and technical training, and the time spent in a program is determined by specialty.   
**4. Pass the Integrated National Board Dental Examination.**To practice, dentists are required to pass the exam and obtain state-specific licensure.  
  
While practicing, each state may require dentists to keep up with changes in ethics, technology and more by taking continuing dental education courses.  
  
Some dentists also specialize, which entails additional training. After completing dental school, these dentists enter residency programs related to a specialty, such as oral or maxillofacial surgery. Programs are often one to two years, but training varies by specialty. Some programs can take up to six years.

## What is a Dentist?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/a43237c/2147483647/thumbnail/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2F02%2Fb5%2F1c3123f449aeb8db06f505ec8710%2Fdentist.jpg)Median Salary$172,790Unemployment Rate N/A Number of Jobs 5,400

Dentists identify and treat problems concerning a patient's mouth, gums and teeth. Their duties include extracting teeth, fitting dentures and filling cavities. Some choose to specialize in areas that range from treating serious oral problems and diseases to straightening teeth and performing oral surgeries. They are assisted by [dental hygienists](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/dental-hygienist "Link: https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/dental-hygienist"), who complete a patient's teeth cleaning, and by [dental assistants](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/dental-assistant "Link: https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/dental-assistant"), who usually help with record keeping and instrument sterilization.  
  
Many people dread the dentist. When they open wide, they're afraid what the dentist will find. Yet another cavity? Or even worse – will it be time for a root canal? Will the dentist embarrass them about their flossing frequency or their coffee drinking? Will they push procedures that patients don't want?  
  
According to Ada S. Cooper, a consumer adviser for the American Dental Association and dentist with a private practice in New York City, these concerns are why establishing trust is so important. "Patients have to know that dentists are doing what's best for them," Cooper says. And they can do this by being honest, ethical and compassionate – three qualities Cooper looks for when she is hiring at her practice. She also highlights the importance of good communication skills.  
  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 4.1% employment growth for dentists between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 5,400 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Dentist

Becoming a dentist involves a marathon of training and testing. Ideally, the pathway starts as early as high school, when you focus on Advanced Placement courses in chemistry, physics, biology and mathematics. Here are the next steps to take:  
  
**1. Get an undergraduate degree.** As undergrads, aspiring dentists will need to take a host of premedical courses in mathematics, chemistry and biology. Aspiring dentists will also need to acquire top marks in undergrad and glowing letters of recommendation to get into dental school.  
**2. Take the Dental Admission Test.** Most dentists take the DAT by their junior year. Getting into dental school is competitive, and scoring well on the acceptance test is only one of the hurdles.  
**3. Attend dental school.**Dental school itself is a rigorous mix of practical and technical training, and the time spent in a program is determined by specialty.   
**4. Pass the Integrated National Board Dental Examination.**To practice, dentists are required to pass the exam and obtain state-specific licensure.  
  
While practicing, each state may require dentists to keep up with changes in ethics, technology and more by taking continuing dental education courses.  
  
Some dentists also specialize, which entails additional training. After completing dental school, these dentists enter residency programs related to a specialty, such as oral or maxillofacial surgery. Programs are often one to two years, but training varies by specialty. Some programs can take up to six years.
